passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof all through the July maths period. "Which jar holds more buttons?" Miss asked. "Hands up for the tall jar." Nearly every hand in the room shot up. Zeenat stared at the short, wide jar. It looked fuller to her. "Zeenat?" Gargi nudged her. "Everybody's saying tall. Just say tall." "But the fat one has more, I think." "If you're wrong, the back bench will laugh at you all week." Zeenat's hand crept up slowly. "Tall," she mumbled. Miss tipped both jars onto the desk and counted aloud. The wide jar won by nine buttons. Gargi gave a small, nervous giggle. "You knew," she whispered. "Why didn't you say?" Zeenat pulled her sleeve over her fingers. "Because everybody else said tall."

qa.q: Which jar did nearly every hand go up for?
qa.a: Nearly every hand shot up for the tall jar.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when she mumbled "Tall"?
qa.a: She felt anxious and small; she believed the wide jar was fuller but was scared the back bench would laugh at her all week if she stood alone and was wrong.

qa.q: What small step could help Zeenat say what she really sees next time?
qa.a: She could give her answer with a reason, like "the wide one looks fuller", and remind herself that being wrong in class is normal and quickly forgotten.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel once the buttons were counted?
qa.a: Gargi's nervous giggle and "Why didn't you say?" suggest she felt awkward, noticing that her push to follow everyone kept Zeenat from giving the right answer.

grounding: Illustrates a child giving the group's answer against what she can see because disagreeing alone feels risky.

passage: It was the week before Holi, and our classroom smelled of the gulal someone had sneaked in. Ma'am held up two paint pots. "If I mix blue and yellow, what do I get?" Maria answered first and loudly. "Purple!" Then the whole row said purple, and the next row too. I knew it was green. I had mixed them in my drawing book a hundred times. But my mouth said "purple" with everyone else. My ears went hot. Ma'am mixed them on a plate. It turned green, of course. Maria laughed and said, "Oops." Nobody laughed at her. I think about that a lot. I, Divyansh, the boy who knew, stayed quiet for nothing.

qa.q: What colour did Maria shout first?
qa.a: Maria answered first and loudly: "Purple!"

qa.q: Why did Divyansh's ears go hot when he said "purple"?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and uneasy, because he knew from his drawing book that blue and yellow make green but went along with the class anyway.

qa.q: What could Divyansh try the next time the class answers together?
qa.a: He could trust what he has tested himself and say "I think it's green, I've mixed it before", even if he is the only one.

qa.q: What would change if Divyansh had said "green" first?
qa.a: Others who also knew might have joined him, and Maria's loud first answer would not have carried the whole class.

grounding: Shows a child copying the class's wrong answer despite seeing the truth, and the risk of disagreeing alone.

passage: Class 3 note, Christmas week. During the paper-star activity I asked, "Which clock shows half past three?" and held up two cardboard clocks. Tarun wrote A on his slate straight away, which was correct. Then he looked around. Most children were writing B, and Dilnaz was already giggling at a friend's slate. Tarun rubbed out his A with his thumb and wrote B. When I asked him later, he said quietly, "I thought A. But everyone put B, and I didn't want them to laugh." What I did next: I praised him for his first answer, privately. The next day I asked the class to answer on slates turned face-down and reveal together, so nobody could copy the crowd.

qa.q: What did Tarun write on his slate at first?
qa.a: He wrote A on his slate straight away, which was correct.

qa.q: What made Tarun rub out his answer, and what was he worried about?
qa.a: He saw most children writing B and Dilnaz giggling, and he felt nervous that they would laugh at him for being different.

qa.q: Which choice by the note-writer worked, and why?
qa.a: Having slates turned face-down and revealed together worked, because children answer before they can see and copy the crowd.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz's giggling look from Tarun's side?
qa.a: To Tarun it may have looked like proof that anyone who differs gets laughed at, even if Dilnaz was only laughing with a friend.

grounding: Illustrates a young child switching to the majority answer out of fear of being laughed at even though his first answer was right.

passage: The touring cinema had packed up by the time the boys reached Bhola's tea stall. "Best film this year," Indu said, blowing on his glass. "That train fight!" Everyone agreed at once. Samir had found the train fight silly; he had nearly dozed off in the second half. He opened his mouth, then shut it. "You liked it, na, Samir?" "Yeah," he heard himself say. "The songs were good." Walking home past the dark mustard fields, he replayed scenes in his head. Maybe the story was cleverer than he had noticed. Maybe he had been too tired. By the time his cousin asked him about it the next morning, Samir was saying, "Best film this year," and he wasn't sure any more if he meant it.

qa.q: Where did the boys go after the touring cinema?
qa.a: They went to Bhola's tea stall.

qa.q: How can you tell that Samir feels unsure of his own opinion by the next morning?
qa.a: He replays scenes wondering if the story was cleverer or if he was too tired, and he repeats "Best film this year" while not sure he means it; he feels doubtful and a little uneasy.

qa.q: What could Samir try the next time his friends all praise something he didn't enjoy?
qa.a: He could say calmly that it wasn't his kind of film and name one part he did like, which keeps his view and the friendship.

qa.q: How might Indu see the evening?
qa.a: Indu probably thinks everyone truly loved the film, never guessing that Samir's quick "Yeah" hid a different view.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a group that unanimously praises a film beginning to doubt his own view and taking on theirs.

passage: In Izmir, the lunch table by the window had rules nobody wrote down. When Jamal walked past with his tray, someone muttered, "Here comes the professor," and the girls snorted. Zeynep had partnered Jamal in chemistry that morning. He had explained the titration slowly, and it was the first time she had understood it. She almost said so. Instead she studied her soup. "He's so weird, right, Zeynep?" She shrugged. "Kind of." All afternoon the word bothered her. Was he weird? He did talk a lot about molecules. Maybe she had been too easy on him. On the bus home, she pictured his patient hands on the burette and felt her face burn. She had not changed her mind. She had just stayed quiet.

qa.q: What did Jamal explain to Zeynep in chemistry that morning?
qa.a: He explained the titration slowly, and it was the first time she understood it.

qa.q: Why did Zeynep's face burn on the bus home?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, because she remembered how kind and patient Jamal had been and knew her "Kind of" had gone along with the table rather than with what she believed.

qa.q: What small step could Zeynep take tomorrow?
qa.a: She could sit with Jamal in chemistry again, or tell one friend at the table that he explained titration really well.

qa.q: If you were Jamal, what might the lunch table feel like?
qa.a: It might feel lonely and unfair to hear jokes about "the professor" and not know that at least one girl there actually valued his help.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager whose group looks down on a classmate, doubting her own view and staying quiet rather than truly changing her mind.

passage: The art room smelled of turpentine on feedback day. Each senior walked the display and ticked one sheet per painting. Simran stopped at a grey, stormy seascape. She loved it; it made her chest tight in a good way. Behind her, Deepika laughed. "Who painted this? It's so muddy." Three seniors nodded. "Totally muddy." "No focal point." Simran looked again. Was it muddy? The waves suddenly seemed smeared, the sky dull. She had written "powerful mood" on her sheet. Her pen hovered. She crossed it out and wrote "colours unclear." Later, alone, she walked past the seascape once more. The storm still pulled at her. She stood there a long minute, unsure which of her two opinions was actually hers.

qa.q: What did Simran first write on her sheet for the seascape?
qa.a: She had written "powerful mood" on her sheet.

qa.q: What is Simran feeling as she stands alone by the seascape?
qa.a: She feels confused and torn, because the painting still moves her, yet after Deepika and the seniors called it muddy she crossed out her praise.

qa.q: What would you advise Simran to do before handing in her sheet?
qa.a: Look once more on her own and write what she honestly notices; she could even note both, like "strong mood, colours a bit unclear".

qa.q: How might the unnamed painter be affected by the feedback sheets?
qa.a: The painter would read a stack of "muddy" comments and never learn that at least one viewer found the work powerful.

grounding: Shows a teenager adopting the group's dismissive view of a painting and doubting her own eyes.

passage: The society's youth committee had one Saturday to plan the playground wall mural. Veer, who always led, unrolled his sketch: black background, neon skulls. "Cool, right?" Heads nodded around the circle. Harsha, sitting by the water tank, noticed how the nods came fast and small. Then Francis scratched his neck. "Honestly? The little kids play there. Skulls might scare them." A pause. Then Mehr said, "I was thinking that too." Then the twins: "Maybe birds? Or the park itself?" Within five minutes the circle was full of ideas that had been hiding. Harsha watched Veer's face shift from annoyance to interest. On the way home, Harsha thought: nobody had disagreed until one person went first.

qa.q: What did Veer's sketch show?
qa.a: A black background with neon skulls.

qa.q: What does Harsha's final thought suggest about how Harsha felt watching the meeting?
qa.a: Harsha felt surprised and a little impressed that the room changed so fast once Francis spoke, realising others had been holding back doubts.

qa.q: How could Harsha use this at the next committee meeting?
qa.a: Harsha could be the first to voice a small, honest doubt, or back someone who does, so others feel safe to speak.

qa.q: What is it like for Francis to speak first against Veer?
qa.a: It is probably nerve-racking; he scratches his neck and hedges with "Honestly?", not knowing anyone will agree.

grounding: Illustrates a teen observing that one person's doubt quickly lets others disagree with the majority.

passage: "So we're agreed," said the group leader, tapping the lab sheet. "Plants grew better in the dark cupboard. Write it up." "Agreed," said two voices. Disha kept her pencil still. Trisha frowned at the numbers. "Wait. Our readings say the window plants grew four centimetres more." Silence. Then the boy by the sink said, "Yeah, I measured those. They're taller." "And the cupboard ones went yellow," another girl added. "I didn't want to say." The leader sighed. "Fine, let's check again." After class, Disha caught up with Trisha on the stairs. "Did you see that? Nobody said anything until you did. Then everybody did." Trisha grinned. "I was shaking." "I couldn't tell," said Disha. "Next time I'll back you faster."

qa.q: How many centimetres more did the window plants grow, according to Trisha?
qa.a: Four centimetres more.

qa.q: What was Disha thinking as she kept her pencil still?
qa.a: She was doubtful and hesitant; she seemed to sense the conclusion was wrong but did not feel brave enough to say it until Trisha spoke.

qa.q: What could Disha do next time to support someone who speaks up?
qa.a: She could back them right away with the evidence she sees, so the first person is not left alone.

qa.q: How does the group leader see Trisha's objection?
qa.a: At first as an annoying delay, shown by the sigh, but the leader accepts it once others agree and says to check again.

grounding: Shows a student observing that a single classmate's doubt lets others dare to disagree with the group.

passage: I'm Kalyani, and last term I was on the prefects' council. At one meeting the head prefect proposed banning Class 8 from the library's back corner because "they're noisy." Every hand went up. Mine too, halfway. Then Aparna said, very softly, "But that's the only place they can sit together. Could we just ask them to keep it down?" I remember the room going still. Then another prefect lowered his hand. Then two more. Within a minute the vote had flipped. I wasn't the one who spoke, but I watched it happen. What stayed with me was how many of us had doubts and needed just one voice before we'd admit them. Now when I disagree, I remember that I might be someone else's one voice.

qa.q: Who did the head prefect want to ban from the library's back corner?
qa.a: Class 8.

qa.q: How can you tell that Kalyani felt unsure before Aparna spoke?
qa.a: Kalyani raised a hand only halfway, which suggests hesitation and unease about the ban even while voting with everyone.

qa.q: What would you advise a prefect who disagrees but fears being alone?
qa.a: Speak up gently with a reason and an alternative, as Aparna did, because others with the same doubt often follow.

qa.q: If you were one of the Class 8 students, what would you want from the council?
qa.a: You would want to be asked to keep quiet rather than banned, and to know someone on the council stood up for your only shared space.

grounding: Illustrates a student noticing that one ally voicing doubt makes it much easier for others to disagree with the majority.

passage: The student society in Utrecht met in a cramped room above the bike shop. "So, the end-of-year party on the canal boat," Astrid said. "All in favour?" Hands went up around the table. Noa kept both hands on the mug. "I'm not sure. Half our new members are exchange students. Many can't afford the ticket, and two told me they can't swim." Heads turned. Someone sighed loudly. Astrid's smile stayed but her voice cooled. "Noted." The vote passed eleven to one. Walking home, Noa kept replaying it. Had it sounded preachy? Were they right that it was just a party? The next week the group chat planned drinks, and Noa's name wasn't tagged. Noa still believed it had been worth saying. It just stung more than expected.

qa.q: What was the vote on the canal boat party?
qa.a: The vote passed eleven to one.

qa.q: What was Noa feeling on the walk home?
qa.a: Noa felt hurt and full of self-doubt, replaying whether the comment sounded preachy, while still believing it was worth saying.

qa.q: What could help Noa after a meeting like this?
qa.a: Noa could talk to one member privately about the exchange students' concern, or suggest a free option alongside the boat.

qa.q: How might Astrid see Noa's objection?
qa.a: Astrid seems to see it as an irritating interruption to a settled plan; her voice cools and she says only "Noted."

grounding: Shows a young adult dissenting alone in a group meeting and feeling stares, pressure, self-doubt and a social cost.

passage: The hostel mess committee met after dinner, the tables still sticky with dal. Francis read the complaint letter aloud: the new cook's food was bland and should be reported to the warden. "Everyone agrees?" Twenty heads nodded. Simran raised a hand. "The cook told me the vegetable budget was cut last month. Maybe we should ask about the budget, not blame him." The room turned to look at her. Someone muttered, "Always has to be different." Francis's pen tapped the table. "We'll put it to a vote." Simran was the only hand against. Back in her room, she stared at the ceiling. Maybe she was naive. Maybe the food really was just bad. But she also thought of the cook's tired face. She didn't sleep well.

qa.q: How many heads nodded when Francis asked if everyone agreed?
qa.a: Twenty heads nodded.

qa.q: Why might Simran have trouble sleeping after the meeting?
qa.a: She feels uneasy and doubtful, wondering if she was naive, while still feeling protective of the tired cook she thinks is being blamed unfairly.

qa.q: How could Simran raise the budget question another way?
qa.a: She could ask the warden directly what changed in the mess budget, or suggest the letter include that question alongside the complaint.

qa.q: What is it like for the cook when the committee blames only him?
qa.a: The cook may feel unfairly judged for something outside his control, and may not know one student tried to explain his side.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who stands alone against a hostel group, facing stares and self-doubt.

passage:
Dear Nitin bhaiya,
You asked why I sounded low on the phone. Here's the whole thing. Our project group of six voted to skip Professor Rao's extra Saturday lecture as a protest about the deadline. I said I'd still go, because the lecture covers the part of the syllabus I don't understand. You should have seen their faces. One of them said, "So you're choosing marks over us." I went. I sat in the second row almost alone, and I kept thinking everyone was right and I was being selfish. Then the professor explained the exact topic I'd been stuck on for weeks. It helped. But in the group chat, nobody answers me quickly anymore. I know I did the right thing for me. It still costs something.
Jyoti

qa.q: What did the project group vote to skip?
qa.a: Professor Rao's extra Saturday lecture.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling while sitting in the second row?
qa.a: Jyoti felt lonely and doubtful, thinking the group might be right and that going was selfish.

qa.q: What could Jyoti try to repair things with the group?
qa.a: Jyoti could offer to share the lecture notes and explain that going was about understanding the topic, not rejecting the protest.

qa.q: How might Nitin read this letter?
qa.a: Nitin might be worried for Jyoti but also proud, seeing the courage it took to go against all six, and might encourage Jyoti to stay steady.

grounding: Shows a young adult as the lone dissenter in a student group, paying a social price and feeling self-doubt though the choice made sense.

passage: The Osaka team had already cheered the new checkout design. "Launch it Monday," Hiroshi said, closing his laptop. Astrid stayed late anyway, pulling last month's test data. The new design had fewer taps, yes. But older users had abandoned it twice as often. She checked the numbers again, then once more with a colleague's sheet. At Friday's stand-up she spoke carefully. "I like the design a lot. May I ask one question first? Why do you think older users dropped off here?" She shared the chart. "I might be reading it wrong." Hiroshi leaned in. Nobody answered for a moment. Then a designer said, "The font size changed." Hiroshi nodded slowly. "Let's test that for a week." Astrid felt her shoulders loosen.

qa.q: When did Hiroshi want to launch the design?
qa.a: Monday.

qa.q: What was Astrid feeling when she said "I might be reading it wrong"?
qa.a: She felt nervous but determined; she had checked carefully yet stayed genuinely open to being wrong, and her shoulders loosened with relief afterwards.

qa.q: Which part of Astrid's approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking a question and showing the chart worked, because it let the team discover the font-size problem themselves instead of feeling attacked.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi see Astrid's question?
qa.a: Hiroshi seems to see it as useful evidence rather than a challenge, since he leans in and agrees to test for a week.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional checking her reasoning, then disagreeing politely with evidence and a question while staying open.

passage: At the community centre, the volunteers planning the blood donation camp had already chalked "Sunday, 8 a.m." on the board. Gurleen, the coordinator, beamed. "Same as every year." Shankar had spent the evening going through last year's sign-up register. He waited for a gap. "Can I share something I found? Last year, most names came after eleven. Many people here work night shifts and sleep early Sunday." He held out the register. "I could be missing something. Was eight chosen for a reason?" Gurleen frowned, then flipped the pages. "Hmm. The doctors prefer mornings." "Maybe nine to one, then?" Shankar offered. Gurleen rubbed out the eight. "Let's ask the doctors about nine." Shankar let out a breath he hadn't noticed holding.

qa.q: What time was chalked on the board at first?
qa.a: "Sunday, 8 a.m."

qa.q: How can you tell that Shankar felt tense about speaking up?
qa.a: He waited for a gap before speaking and let out a breath he hadn't noticed holding, which shows he was nervous and relieved once it went well.

qa.q: How could other volunteers learn from the way Shankar raised it?
qa.a: They could check facts first, ask why a plan was chosen, and offer a middle option, as Shankar did with nine to one.

qa.q: Why might Gurleen react differently if Shankar had just said "Eight is wrong"?
qa.a: Gurleen might have felt criticised and defended the tradition instead of looking at the register and considering the doctors' view.

grounding: Shows a young adult checking evidence, then disagreeing politely with a question and a suggestion while staying open to being wrong.

passage:
Subject: Help pages in Hindi, a question before we decide

Hi Bhupen,

I know the team agreed on Tuesday to drop the Hindi help pages next quarter to save writing time, and I understand why. Before it's final, I went through three months of support tickets. About a third of our "can't log in" tickets come from users who first opened the Hindi pages. If those pages vanish, I wonder whether those tickets will rise. I've attached the sheet so you can check my counting; I may have tagged some wrongly. Could we keep only the five most-visited Hindi pages for one quarter and compare? If the numbers say I'm wrong, I'm happy to drop it.

Thanks for hearing me out,
Tushar

qa.q: What did the team agree on Tuesday?
qa.a: To drop the Hindi help pages next quarter to save writing time.

qa.q: What does Tushar's line "I may have tagged some wrongly" suggest about how Tushar feels?
qa.a: It suggests Tushar feels cautious and humble; Tushar is confident enough to raise the point but genuinely open to being wrong.

qa.q: What went well in how Tushar disagreed, and what could make it even stronger?
qa.a: Tushar offered evidence, a small trial and a way to be proven wrong; talking to one teammate first might make it stronger still.

qa.q: How might Bhupen feel receiving this email?
qa.a: Bhupen might feel respected rather than challenged, because the email acknowledges the team's reasons and offers data to check.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional who checks the reasoning first, then disagrees politely with evidence and stays open to being wrong.

passage: Diwali evening, and the flat glowed with diyas. "One for Samir!" Vaibhav pushed a laddoo into his little brother's fist. "One for Dadi!" Dadi pretended to faint with joy. Then the new neighbours came in with a girl in a sparkly frock. She looked at the box. Vaibhav slid it behind his back. Mummy crouched. "She's our guest." He looked at the girl's shoes, then at Samir chewing happily. Slowly he held up the smallest laddoo. The girl took it and smiled. Vaibhav smiled back, just a little.

qa.q: What was the first thing Vaibhav gave Samir?
qa.a: He pushed a laddoo into his little brother's fist.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav slide the box behind his back?
qa.a: He felt shy and unsure about the new girl; sharing with his brother and Dadi felt easy, but a stranger's child felt different and he was reluctant.

qa.q: How could Mummy help Vaibhav share with new people next time?
qa.a: She could introduce the guest by name and let the children play first, so the stranger feels familiar before sharing.

qa.q: What might the girl in the sparkly frock feel when the box disappears?
qa.a: She might feel left out and shy in a new home, and then pleased when she finally gets a laddoo.

grounding: Shows a young child sharing readily with his brother and grandmother but more slowly with a visiting child.

passage: It was the hottest week of May. "Hemant Nanu, one for you!" Ishita held out a whole slice of mango. "Only if you eat one too," Nanu laughed. A boy from the next bench in the park stood watching, thumb in his mouth. "Ishita, he's looking at the mangoes." "He's not our family." "Does that mean he can't have any?" Ishita hugged the box. "I don't know him." "You could ask his name." "What's your name?" she called. The boy mumbled. She put one small piece on a leaf and held it out at arm's length.

qa.q: What did Ishita hold out to Hemant Nanu?
qa.a: She held out a whole slice of mango.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when she hugged the mango box?
qa.a: She felt wary and protective; the boy was a stranger, and sharing with someone who wasn't family made her hesitant.

qa.q: What small step did Nanu suggest to help Ishita share?
qa.a: He suggested she ask the boy's name, which makes a stranger feel less strange.

qa.q: How might the boy from the next bench see Ishita's piece on a leaf?
qa.a: He might feel pleased but still shy, noticing it came at arm's length and that she shared much more easily with Nanu.

grounding: Illustrates a young child who shares freely with her grandfather but hesitates with an unknown child.

passage: Nursery note, January winter picnic. Jatin's cousin Mohit visited today. At snack time Jatin pushed half his orange across the mat to Mohit: "This is my brother-cousin." Later a girl who joined this week sat near Jatin. He turned his back and ate his segments quickly. I didn't force sharing. I sat with both and said, "This is Tia. She likes oranges too." Jatin stared, then offered one segment, fast, and looked at me. Next steps: pair Jatin with Tia for garden jobs so they get to know each other.

qa.q: What did Jatin call Mohit?
qa.a: "My brother-cousin."

qa.q: What might Jatin have been feeling when he turned his back on the new child?
qa.a: He probably felt shy and wary, because the new child was unfamiliar to him while Mohit was family.

qa.q: Why might pairing Jatin with Tia for garden jobs help?
qa.a: Spending time together can make Tia feel familiar to Jatin, and children share more easily with people they feel close to.

qa.q: What is it like for Tia when Jatin turns his back?
qa.a: Tia may feel left out and uncertain in her first week, watching someone share with one child and not with her.

grounding: Shows a young child sharing easily with a cousin and more slowly with an unfamiliar child.

passage: Monsoon mornings meant one umbrella for two, and that morning Nitin and Damini fought over it all the way to the gate. "You always hold it on your side!" "Because I'm taller!" She stomped ahead, soaked, and ignored him all day. At the bus stop after school, two older boys circled her. "Wet cat," one sneered, flicking water at her bag. Damini's chin wobbled. Nitin didn't think. He pushed between them and opened the umbrella over her. "Leave my sister alone." His voice cracked but he stood there. The boys shrugged and wandered off. The bus conductor said, "Next time, tell a teacher too, beta." At home, Mama heard the story and wrote to the class teacher that evening. Damini shared the umbrella on the walk home.

qa.q: What did Nitin and Damini fight over that morning?
qa.a: They fought over the umbrella.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when his voice cracked?
qa.a: He was scared of the older boys but felt fiercely protective of Damini, so his loyalty beat both his fear and the morning's anger.

qa.q: How could Nitin handle bullying like this next time?
qa.a: Along with standing by his sister, he could tell a teacher, as the conductor suggested, so an adult deals with the older boys.

qa.q: How might Damini see her brother after the bus stop?
qa.a: She might feel protected and grateful, seeing that he stood up for her even though they had fought all day.

grounding: Illustrates a child defending his sister from bullies even after quarrelling with her that morning.

passage: "You broke my kite reel!" Nikita shouted before breakfast on Sankranti morning. "It was already broken!" Sachin shouted back. By noon they were flying separate kites from opposite ends of the terrace. Then a bigger boy from the next building leaned over the wall and yanked Nikita's string. "This is mine now." "Give it back!" Nikita's eyes filled. Sachin dropped his own kite. "That's my sister's. Give it back." "Or what?" "Or I'm getting Uncle from downstairs right now." The boy glanced toward the stairs. He threw the kite onto the terrace. Sachin picked it up and handed it to her. "Still angry about the reel?" she sniffed. "Yes," he said. "Doesn't matter." Uncle from downstairs came up anyway and spoke to the boy's parents.

qa.q: What did Nikita accuse Sachin of before breakfast?
qa.a: Breaking her kite reel.

qa.q: How can you tell Sachin was still upset with Nikita even as he helped her?
qa.a: When she asks if he's still angry about the reel, he says "Yes"; he still feels resentful but his protective loyalty matters more.

qa.q: Which part of Sachin's response worked, and why?
qa.a: Saying he would fetch Uncle from downstairs worked, because the bigger boy knew an adult would step in.

qa.q: What would change if Sachin had kept flying his own kite?
qa.a: Nikita would have faced the bigger boy alone, and she might have learned that their fight counted for more than being family.

grounding: Shows a child defending his sister from a bully despite their quarrel that morning.

passage: In the summer holidays, Darshan and I share one bicycle, and that morning he took it without asking. I shouted at him so loudly that Mummy came out. We weren't speaking at lunch. In the evening I went to the ground and saw a bigger boy holding my brother's shoe up high. "Torn shoes, torn shoes," he was singing. Darshan was trying not to cry. I forgot about the bicycle. I walked straight up, even though the boy was a head taller. "Give it back to him." He laughed, but he dropped it. I'm Gautam, Darshan's big brother, and my knees were shaking. When we got home I told Mummy, and she went to the boy's house that same evening. Darshan still takes the bicycle sometimes. I let him.

qa.q: What was the bigger boy singing?
qa.a: "Torn shoes, torn shoes."

qa.q: How was Gautam feeling as he walked up to the bigger boy?
qa.a: Gautam was afraid, since his knees were shaking, but he felt fiercely protective and forgot his anger about the bicycle.

qa.q: What did Gautam do after they got home, and why did it help?
